work.title: De Benedictionibus Patriarcharum Liber Unus

paragraphs.text: First of all, how great a reverence we learn to show our parents when we read that whoever was blessed by his father was blessed, and whoever was cursed was cursed! God gave parents this privilege so that children's devotion might be called forth. The parents' prerogative, then, is the training of their children. So honour your father, that he may bless you. Let the devoted son honour his father out of gratitude, the ungrateful one out of fear. Even if the father is poor and has no wealth to leave his children, he still has the inheritance of his last blessing, by which he can bestow the riches of sanctification on those who come after him. And it is far more to become blessed than to become rich.

Joseph was eager to receive the blessing. So he even brought his sons Manasseh and Ephraim, and Jacob blessed them. Since Jacob had twelve sons, and Paul was to be the thirteenth apostle, chosen as it were later, a thirteenth tribe was to be sanctified from his grandsons Manasseh and Ephraim, divided between the two. In this way Paul would not be found outside the number of the ancestral tribes; as the outstanding preacher of both the Old and the New Testament, he could readily show that the inheritance of the ancestral blessing had come to benefit him as well.

What splendid mysteries there are in this! Joseph took his sons, whom he had begotten in Egypt, Ephraim at his own right hand, which was Israel his father's left, and Manasseh at his own left, which was Israel's right, and brought them near before his father. But Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, who was the younger and stood at his grandfather's left, and laid his left hand on Manasseh, who was at his right; and so, with his hands crossed, he blessed them. In this Joseph kept the order of nature, so as to give more to the elder son, just as Isaac too wished to confer the blessing on Esau, his firstborn son. But Jacob believed that the younger son should be preferred, as a type of the younger people, just as he himself had been preferred by his mother.

Manasseh, in Latin translation, means "from forgetfulness," because the people of the Jews forgot their God who made them, and whoever of that people comes to believe is called back, as it were, from forgetfulness. Ephraim, by the meaning of his name, promises fruitfulness of faith, he who increased his father, as Joseph himself says: "For God has increased me in the land of my humiliation." This is proper to the younger people, which is the body of Christ, increasing the Father and not forsaking its own God.

Indeed, the old man made it plain that this mystery concerns the peoples in a spiritual sense. For when his son thought he had made a mistake through the failing of his dimmer sight, and wanted to shift his hands, saying, "Not so, father, for this one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head," he refused and said: "I know, my son, I know. This one too shall become a people, and this one too shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations." He also prophesied, by the very order of the blessing, that Ephraim was to be preferred to his elder brother, saying: "In you shall Israel be blessed, when they say, 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.'" And so, though they were grandsons, they were adopted in the place of sons, so that they should not be left without a share in their grandfather's blessing.

When this blessing had been given, he also called his sons. And he who had earlier set the younger before the elder now began with the first, so that in the former case he might give preference to the grace of the mystery, and in this one keep the order of age. At the same time, because he had earlier blessed them all in those two, together with all their posterity and the offspring of those yet to come, he did not want a repeated blessing of the people to seem superfluous, or the earlier one to be thought weak. And so he rightly says that what he is now conferring is a proclamation of what was to happen in later times rather than a repeated blessing.

So he began thus: "Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sons, hard to bear and hard and reckless; you have done outrage. Do not boil over like water, for you went up to your father's bed; then you defiled the couch on which you went up." Does he not seem to be rebuking rather than blessing? And that is why it is a prophecy rather than a blessing. For a prophecy is the announcement of things to come, while a blessing is the prayerful bestowal of sanctification and graces.

The Jews think that the old man says this to his son Reuben because he lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and defiled his father's bed. But they are easily refuted, for that had been done earlier, whereas Jacob promises that he will tell what is to come in the last days, not what had already been done. So the patriarch's statement is consistent and coherent: foreseeing the Lord's future passion at the hands of the persecuting Jews, he curses the monstrous audacity of the firstborn people, which, unbelieving and not subject to the law of God, and with a stiff neck not knowing how to bear the yoke of Christ, assailed the Author of life not only with the crime of murder but also with the outrage of sacrilegious mockery.

"Do not boil over like water," he says, so that the people may not break out into greater madness, and the heat of fury and insanity may not keep the sinners from coming to their senses, but they may do penance for their offences. For the hard people went up to the father's bed and defiled the holy couch, that is, by fastening to the gibbet of the cross the flesh of the Lord Jesus, our Creator, on which, as on a kind of bed and father's couch, his saints rest in saving refreshment. Who then would deny that this was said of the people, since all these things fit the people? For it was called Israel the firstborn; it was called stiff-necked; of it Moses said: "But you are a stiff-necked people." And truly, who is so hard, so reckless and so insolent as the people of the Jews, who scourged the Lord Jesus and fastened him with nails, though through him they had seen the dead raised and the blind given light, and though they could not deny his divine works? The narrative of the gospel has made clear that this was committed at the instigation of the scribes and chief priests, with Caiaphas, the high priest, raging along with them. And so the holy prophet shrank from any share in so great a crime, so that through descent from him they might not dare to claim fellowship with so great a patriarch.

The righteous man calls witnesses and disowns a posterity that would not keep their father's disposition; and because he foresaw the outrage, he shudders at the contagion of their counsel. "Let my soul not come into their counsel," he says, "and let my inmost being not contend in their assembly, for in their anger they killed a man and in their lust they hamstrung a bull." What he says, he says of his sons Simeon and Levi; but under their names he signifies the tribes that were called by the same names. The Jews turn aside this most beautiful interpretation and think that Jacob rebukes his sons because, on account of the rape of their sister, these two, wanting more than the other brothers to take revenge on the Shechemites, pretended that they wished to enter into friendship with them, and therefore persuaded them that they must be circumcised, so that peace between them and a bond of intermarriage might be confirmed by a common religion. But they attacked the circumcised men while their wounds were still fresh and their strength weak, sapped by pain, and on the third day they slew them in their broken state. And perhaps these two were the avengers above the others because they are the founders of the scribes and the priests; for no one ought to defend chastity more than the wise and the priests.

But in this too the Jews are mistaken. For these two had set before their father the reasons for their grief, declaring that, though at a youthful age, they had been the avengers of wounded family honour and of violated chastity [?]. This holy Jacob certainly could not condemn, since they did not allow their sister to be treated as a harlot, she who had lost her virginity and had no consolation of vengeance. All the more so since he himself approved of the deed: when he possessed Shechem, he gave it at his death to his most beloved son Joseph, saying to him: "I give you Shechem, as a special portion above all your brothers, which I took from the hands of the Amorites with my sword and bow." This deed cannot be denied, but we can interpret it: Shechem signifies shoulders, and shoulders signify works. So he chose holy Joseph above the rest as heir of good works, for his brothers could not equal his works.

For who could equal the deeds of Christ? Moreover, spotless and chaste, he carried off spoils from this earthly lodging and from the authors of impurity, taking with heavenly words and a spiritual sword a place given over to debauchery and crime and making it a dwelling for the saints. So where once the denizens of wantonness and the princes of luxury moved about, where there had been the incitements of lust and the kindling of wickedness, there now holy priests teach the lessons of chastity, and many examples of virginal purity shine with a kind of radiance of heavenly light.

So it is tribes that are designated by the names of the patriarchs, for from the tribe of Simeon come the scribes, and from the tribe of Levi the chief priests, who brought their wickedness to completion in the Lord's passion, filling up the whole measure of their fathers' impiety. They devised a plan against the Lord Jesus to kill him, as Isaiah says: "Woe to their soul, for they have devised an evil plan against themselves, saying: Let us bind the righteous one, for he is useless to us." They killed the prophets and apostles who announced the coming of the saving Lord and proclaimed the glory of his passion and resurrection. Afterwards, in their lust, because they desired earthly vices and fled from the fellowship of divine things, chastity of body, sobriety of mind, contempt of money and the gain of grace, they hamstrung the bull, that is, the one that puts forth horns and hoofs, whom the poor see and rejoice, because by the word of God he has exalted the horn of his people, with which he both drove back his enemies and won the reward of the heavenly crown. This is the bull by which the Church is figured: in the moon, which is then at its fullest when, resting as it were on the horns of the bull, it encloses the expanse of the whole world.

Yet he seems to join to this prophecy the grace of a blessing as well. For in saying to Reuben, the firstborn, "Do not boil over like water," he checked sin, since water is more accustomed to cleanse offences and to recall our minds from every heat of vice. And again, in saying to Simeon and Levi, "I will divide you in Jacob and scatter you in Israel," he showed that they were to be redeemed through the gathering of the nations. For when the shepherd was struck, the flock that had earlier been gathered was scattered, so that one who was not of it might come in, and so all Israel might be saved. We ought to believe this especially on account of the tribe of Levi, because the Lord Jesus appears to derive his lineage from that tribe according to the body he assumed. From this tribe come the priests Levi and Nathan, whom Saint Luke, in the book of the gospel that he wrote, counted among the Lord's forebears. For the priest of the Father and prince of all priests, as it is written, "You are a priest for ever," had to claim succession from a priestly origin.

That is why Moses too blessed this tribe, saying: "Give to Levi the lot of his choosing, and his truth to the holy man." Moses also blessed the tribe of Reuben, as you have it written: "Let Reuben live and not die, and let him be many in number." He would not have blessed them if he had known them to be unworthy of blessing according to the patriarch's pronouncement. Certainly, what the one passed over briefly, the other filled out.
And because the tribes of Judah and Levi were joined by intermarriage, Matthew traces his family from the tribe of Judah.

And the apostle says that our Lord arose from Judah. So from the tribe of Levi a priestly inheritance, full of holiness, is reckoned to him, while from the tribe of Judah, from which David and Solomon and the other kings came, the splendour of royal succession shines out, so that the testimony of the Scriptures shows the same one to be both king and priest. Rightly, then, did holy Jacob pour himself out on the grace of Judah, saying: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be on the back of your enemies; your father’s sons shall bow down to you. Judah is a lion’s whelp. From a shoot, my son, you have gone up for me. Lying down, you slept like a lion and like a whelp: who will rouse him? A judge shall not be lacking from Judah, nor a prince from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up, and he is the expectation of the nations. He binds his she-ass to the vine and his ass’s colt to the haircloth. He will wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape. His eyes are merry from wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.”

The address seems to be directed to the patriarch Judah, but it portrays that later Judah, the true Confessor, who was born of that tribe. He alone is praised by his brothers, of whom he says: “I will tell your name to my brothers.” He is Lord by nature and brother by grace. His hands, which he stretched out to an unbelieving people, are on the back of his enemies. With those same hands and that same passion he protected his own, subdued the hostile powers, and made subject to himself all who have no part in faith and piety. Of these the Father says to the Son: “And you shall rule in the midst of your enemies.” It was their own malice that made them enemies, not the will of Christ. In this lies the great grace of the Lord. For the spiritual forces of wickedness used to bend our neck under the yoke of captivity, so that David himself wrote that he could, as it were, feel the hands of those triumphing over him: “Sinners built upon my back.” Now those same forces are subject to Christ’s triumph and, in a way, to his hands, that is, to his deeds and works, and they undergo the misery of perpetual captivity. He it is, surely, who is worshipped by his father’s sons when he is worshipped by us, for he has allowed us to call his Father our Father. To be his servant is itself a mark of virtue.

“Judah is a lion’s whelp.” Has he not plainly indicated the Father and declared the Son? What could be plainer as a lesson that the Son is God of one nature with the Father? The one is a lion, the other a lion’s whelp. By a humble comparison we understand that they are one in nature and power. King came forth from King, Strong from Strong. Because he foresaw that some would claim the Son is younger, he meets them by adding: “From a shoot you have gone up for me. Lying down, you slept like a lion and like a whelp.” And elsewhere you read that the whelp himself is the lion of the tribe of Judah. Because he had said “whelp,” then, he rightly added “lion” at once. It is as if he said: “Do not let your ears be misled because they heard ‘whelp.’ I have indicated the Son, but I did not say that he is lesser. He too is a lion, as the Father is.” Let them hear that he called him both lion and whelp: lion as having perfect and full power, whelp as being the Son. So no one who hears it should think that the Son is not equal to the Father. The Son is not praised in a way that separates him from the Father.

He who confesses the Son proves him equal. Wonderfully, too, he described his incarnation when he said: “From a shoot you have gone up for me.” For like a shrub of the earth he sprouted in the Virgin’s womb, and like a sweet-smelling flower he went up for the redemption of the whole world, sent forth from his mother’s womb in the splendour of a new light. As Isaiah says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall go up from the root.” The root is the family of the Jews, the rod is Mary, and the flower of Mary is Christ. She is rightly called a rod, for she is of royal stock, of the house and family of David. Her flower [?] is Christ, who did away with the stench of the world’s filth and poured in the fragrance of eternal life.

You have the incarnation, then; now hear of the passion. “Lying down,” he says, “you slept like a lion.” This was when he lay in the tomb, at rest as though in a kind of sleep of his body, as he himself says: “I slept and took my rest and rose up, because the Lord will uphold me.” Hence Jacob also says: “Who will rouse him?” That is: the one whom the Lord will uphold. Who else could raise him up, unless he raised himself by his own power and his Father’s? I see him born by his own authority, I see him dead by his own will, I see him asleep by his own power. He did all things by his own choice. Whose help will he need in order to rise? He himself, then, is the author of his resurrection, for he is the master of death. He is the one the nations await.

So a leader shall not fail from Judah until he comes, so that the royal succession might be kept faithful and uncorrupted up to his birth. For afterwards, as we showed in our treatise on the Gospel, the succession was corrupted through Herod and lost the privilege of its dignity. Because they rejected the true king, they began to have false ones. This, then, is what the patriarch is saying: the inheritance of an unbroken succession, passed down through the kings, will be preserved among the judges or kings of the Jews until he comes for whom it is laid up. He will gather the church of God from the assembly of all nations and the devotion of the Gentile peoples. That is, it awaits him, what is owed is kept for him, and to him is given the privilege of so great a grace.

“And he is the expectation of the nations.” He said more than if he had said, “The nations await him,” for all the hope of the church rests in him. That is why Moses was told: “Loose the sandal from your feet.” He was being chosen as leader of the people, and he was not to be thought the bridegroom of the church. That is why Joshua son of Nun loosed his sandal: he too was keeping the grace of so great an office for the one who was to come. That is why John says: “After me comes a man the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to loose.” That is why he says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy.” That is: He alone is the husband of the church. He is the expectation of the nations. To him the prophets yielded the bond of nuptial grace, and so they loosed their sandals. He is the bridegroom; I am the bridegroom’s friend. I rejoice because he has come, because I hear the voice of the wedding. Now we hear no longer the harsh punishments of sinners and the harsh torments of the law, but the forgiveness of crimes, the voice of gladness, the sound of joy, the exultation of the wedding feast.

He is the one who binds his ass to the vine and his ass’s colt to the haircloth. So the assembly of the nations, once slack and negligent but now devoted through Christ, may have the fervour of the Holy Spirit. And so we may be bound to that everlasting vine, that is, to the Lord Jesus, who says, “I am the vine; my Father is the vinedresser.” We are bound to him like fruitful branches, by bonds of faith that cannot be loosed. This is the mystery by which he ordered in the Gospel that the ass’s colt be untied, and the Lord Jesus himself sat on it, so that, bound to the vine, it might rest in the everlasting sweetness of the saints.

“He will wash,” he says, “his robe in wine.” The flesh of Christ is a good robe. It covered the sins of all, took on the offences of all, and hid the errors of all. It is a good robe, which clothed everyone in the garment of joy. He washed this robe in wine when he was baptized in the Jordan and the Holy Spirit descended like a dove and remained on him. This signifies that the fullness of the Holy Spirit was in him undivided and did not leave him. Hence the evangelist also says that the Lord Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. Jesus therefore washed his robe, not to wash away filth of his own, for there was none, but to wash away ours, which there was. Then he added: “and his cloak in the blood of the grape.” That is, in the passion of his body he washed the nations clean with his blood. For the nations are the cloak of the Word, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, I will surely clothe myself with them all as with a garment.” And elsewhere: “Like a mantle you will change them, and they will be changed.” So with his own blood he cleansed not his own sins, for there were none, but the offences that we committed. And rightly he said “grape” [?], because he hung on the wood like a grape. He is the vine and he is the grape: the vine because he clung to the wood, the grape because his side, opened by the soldier’s lance, poured out water and blood. For John said that water and blood came out of him: the water for washing, the blood for the price. The water washes us; the blood has redeemed us.

And so the prophet says: “His eyes are merry from wine and his teeth whiter than milk.” By this he means the prophets and the apostles. Some, like the eyes of Christ, foresaw and announced his coming. Of them he himself says: “Abraham saw my day and was glad.” And one of the prophets says: “I saw the Lord of hosts.” Seeing him, they were filled with spiritual gladness. Others, that is, the apostles, were cleansed by the Lord from every stain of sin and made whiter than milk, and no stain darkened them afterwards. For milk is temporal, but the grace of the apostles lasts forever. They prepared for us those spiritual and heavenly foods and fattened the inmost parts of the inner mind. Some also think that the Lord’s bright commandments, which came from the divine mouth, have become like milk for us, and that, nourished by them, we come to the nourishment of the heavenly bread. Hence Paul too says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able.” The Corinthian, at the beginning of his faith, is given milk to drink. But those saints whose faith is proclaimed in the whole world are, like weaned children, strengthened with more solid food.

“Zebulun shall dwell by the sea, and he by the harbour of ships, and he shall stretch as far as Sidon.” The very meaning of the name promises better things, for in Latin it means “deliverance from things of the night.” This is surely a good thing, and it belongs to the one who hopes under the wings of the Lord, whose truth surrounds him, so that he need not fear the terror of the night or the thing that prowls in darkness.

This Zebulun, then, he says, shall dwell by the sea. There he may see the shipwrecks of others while he himself is safe from danger, and watch others tossed about on the strait of this world, carried around by every wind of doctrine, while he stays immovable, rooted in faith. So it is with the holy church: rooted and grounded in faith, she watches the storms of the heretics and the shipwrecks of the Jews, who rejected the helmsman they once had. She dwells beside the waves but is not shaken by them; she is more ready to help than exposed to danger. If any who are driven by heavy storms wish to flee to harbour, the church is there as a harbour of salvation. With outstretched arms she calls those in peril into the lap of her calm and shows them a place of safe anchorage. The churches in this world, then, are like seaports spread along the shores. They come to meet those in distress and tell them that a refuge has been prepared for believers, where ships battered by the winds can be drawn up.

In these churches are the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali, as Psalm 67 teaches. Some of them are deliverers from the storm of the night, crying: “Let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light.” Others have the breadth of the apostles and can say: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is opened wide.” These are the ones who, when they were in darkness, saw a great light, as the prophet testifies: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan: the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light. For those who sat in the region of the shadow of death, a light has risen.”

So the Lord our God has set the heirs of this patriarch as watchmen by the harbour of ships. Their wakeful care and spiritual succession stretch as far as Sidon, that is, they reach to the Gentiles, so that the mercy of the Lord may lift away the sins of the nations. For Sidon is the firstborn son of Ham, the Ham who was condemned by his father’s curse for his irreverence toward the respect owed a father. Deliverance from the night, then, is stationed on watch as on a spiritual rampart, so that no one may run onto the rocks of this life. It stretches as far as those guilty of the gravest crimes, even to the Sidonians themselves, whose name, as its meaning shows, once called them “hunters of crimes” because of their fierce superstition. It sets them free: the inheritance of the curse is dissolved and the inheritance of the blessing is given, so that where the guilt was greater, grace may now be more abundant.

“Issachar desired what is good, resting between the lots. And seeing that rest is good and that the land is rich, he put his shoulder to labour and became a farmer.” Issachar means “reward,” and so it refers to Christ, who is our reward, since we buy him for ourselves, toward the hope of eternal salvation, not with gold and silver but with faith and devotion. Hence David says of him: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons; the reward is the fruit of the womb.” And Moses says of him: “The reward of those who dwell by the sea.” He is the one who desired the good from the beginning and did not know how to desire what is evil. Isaiah too says of him: “Before the child knows how to call father or mother, he does not trust in wickedness, choosing what is good.” He rested between the lots of the Old and New Testaments, or in the midst of the prophets. That is why he appeared in the middle, between Moses and Elijah. It showed us that he has rest in the words of those through whom many renounce their sins and believe in the living God. Or else it showed that they themselves are witnesses of his resurrection and blessed rest.

And so, to call the nations to the grace of his resurrection, he put his shoulder to labour, submitting himself to the cross in order to carry our sins. For the nations are that rich and fertile land, which yields eternal fruits, fruits a hundredfold and sixtyfold. That is why the prophet says: “whose government is upon his shoulder.” That is, the power of the divinity rests upon the passion of the body, or the cross towers over the body. So he set his shoulder to it, bending over the plough, patient in undergoing every insult. He was so given over to labour that he was wounded for our iniquities and made weak for our sins. And he became a farmer, who knows how to sow his land with good grain and to plant fruit trees with deep roots.

“Dan shall judge his people as one tribe of Israel. And Dan became for him a serpent sitting by the way, biting the horse’s heel on the path, and the rider shall fall backward, awaiting salvation from the Lord.” Taken simply, this means that the tribe of Dan also gave a judge to Israel. For after Joshua son of Nun there were judges of the people from various tribes, and Samson, who was of the tribe of Dan, judged for twenty years. But the prophecy does not mean him. It means the Antichrist, who will come from the tribe of Dan and judge the people as a cruel judge and monstrous tyrant. Like a serpent sitting by the way, he will try to throw down those who walk the way of truth, wanting to trip up the truth. This is what biting the horse’s heel means: the horse, struck by the spreading venom and wounded by the serpent’s tooth, lifts its heel. So Judas the betrayer, tempted by the devil, lifted his heel against the Lord Jesus, to throw down the Rider who had lowered himself to lift everyone up. He fell, then, not flat on his face like one dozing, but backward, stretching from the things above to what lay ahead, and awaiting salvation from the Lord. For he knew that he would be raised again, and so he was waiting to lift up fallen Adam.

So when we are running well on the way, let us take care that no serpent is lurking somewhere on the path to undercut the footing of the horse, that is, of our body, and suddenly throw down the rider while he sleeps. For if we keep awake, we should be able to guard ourselves to some extent and avoid the serpent’s bites. Do not let the sleep of negligence overcome us, the sleep of the world; do not let the sleep of riches overcome us, or it may be said of us too: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing.” But there are also sleeping riders, of whom it is written: “Those who mounted horses have dozed off.” If greed wounds your heart, if lust inflames it, you are a sleeping rider, and so you cannot rein in your body, that is, your horse. Stay awake, then, so that even if you have been thrown down, that is, even if you have died, you may not fall asleep. For those who sleep their sleep find nothing. But you must await salvation from the Lord and look for it as it comes, so that you may find the grace of resurrection. Judas was asleep; indeed, he did not hear the words of Christ. Judas was asleep, and it was the sleep of riches, for he sought payment for his betrayal. The devil saw him asleep and weighed down by the heavy sleep of greed. He thrust himself into his heart, wounded the horse, and threw down the rider, whom he cut off from Christ.

Moses blessed this tribe, saying: “Dan is a lion’s whelp, and he shall escape from Bashan,” that is, from shame. So, following the Greek from which the Latin was translated, we ought rather to understand that Dan himself became a serpent sitting by the way. Dan means “judgment,” and so this tribe has undergone the grave peril of judgment. The serpent that slipped into it is the Antichrist, who was to wound the runner with his venom. Yet this tribe will be delivered from shame when it has confessed the Rider who rose again, who says: “Whoever is ashamed of me before men, I too will put him to shame before my Father, who is in heaven. But whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father, who is in heaven.”

“Gad: temptation shall tempt him, and he shall tempt them at their feet.” The temptation is the gathering and the cunning of the scribes and priests. As Scripture has shown, they tempted the Lord Jesus about the tribute to Caesar and about John’s baptism, and the Lord Jesus, in his justice, turned their test back on them. “At their feet” means replying on the spot, without any deliberation, so as to hem in his tempters all the more. For when they said, “By what authority do you do these things?”, he did not answer their question but put one of his own, saying: “I too will ask you one thing. If you tell me, I too will tell you by what authority I do these things.” Again, when they said, “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?”, he said: “Why do you test me, you hypocrites? Show me the coin for the tax.” When they brought it, he asked in turn: “Whose image and inscription is this?” They said to him: “Caesar’s.” There he bound them by their own words and held them by their own admission. Then he said to them: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s,” so that they could not go against their own words. And so they marvelled and went away from him. But it is no wonder that he answered “at their feet,” since he saw what lay before their feet.

Moses showed clearly that this prophecy of holy Jacob is about Christ, for he says: “Blessed is he who enlarged Gad. Like a lion he rested, breaking arms and princes. And he saw from his beginning that there the land of the princes was divided, gathered together with the princes of the peoples. The Lord has done justice and judgment for Israel.”

So we recognize who it was that rested like a lion when he broke the arms of the mighty, for from the beginning he saw the divisions of those who tempted him. There, then, where the faithless do their tempting, the earth gapes open to swallow the slanderers.

“Asher: his bread is rich, and he shall give food to princes.” In Latin, Asher means “riches.” Who, then, is rich, if not where there is the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God? Who is rich but the Lord Jesus, who always abounds and never runs short? He came poor into this world and was abundant for all; he filled everyone. How great are his riches, when by his poverty he made all rich! He was poor for our sake, but rich with the Father. He was poor in order to rescue us from want, as the apostle teaches: “For your sake he became poor, though he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich.” His poverty makes rich, his fringe heals, his hunger satisfies, his death gives life, his burial raises up. This, then, is the rich treasure whose bread is rich. And it is rightly called rich, for whoever eats it can never hunger. This bread he gave to the apostles to share out among the people of believers, and today he gives it to us: the bread which the priest himself consecrates daily with his words.

This bread, then, has become the food of the saints. We may also take it to mean the Lord himself, who gave us his flesh, as he himself says: “I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the desert and died; but this is the bread that came down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die.” Someone might think he was speaking of the death that comes when soul and body are separated, and might rightly have doubts, since he knows that the holy apostles died that death. So the Lord added: “I am the living bread, who came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this will live forever.” That is: I was not speaking above of temporal life, or of the death of this life. Even if someone dies that death, if he has received my bread, he will live forever. For he receives it who examines himself, and whoever receives it will not die the death of a sinner, because this bread is the forgiveness of sins.

Moses too prophesied most beautifully in his blessings, saying: “Blessed above sons is Asher, and he shall be pleasing to his brothers, and he shall dip his foot in oil. Iron and bronze shall be his sandal, and as your days are, so shall your strength be. There is none like your God in heaven, your helper, great and the beauty of the firmament, God of the beginning who protects you, and through the strength of mighty arms. And he shall drive out the enemy from before your face, saying: ‘Perish!’ And Israel shall dwell in confidence, alone, on the land of Jacob, with grain and wine, and heaven shall be yours with a cloud of dew.”

Naphtali is a vine let loose, putting forth beauty in its offspring. One shoot of the vine is cut off because it seems useless, so that the vine does not run riot in a fruitless profusion of shoots; another is cut back a little and then let loose to bear fruit, and its beauty is put forth in what it brings forth. For as it lifts itself up toward the heights, it embraces the vine, and climbing to the top of the trellis it clothes, as it were, the necks of the vines with a necklace of precious branches. That shoot too shows beauty in what it brings forth, because its branches are full and overflow with abundant fruit.

This is a fine sight, but far more beautiful is what it signifies: the branch clinging to the spiritual vine. We are its shoots, and we can bear fruit if we remain in the vine; if not, we are cut off.

The holy patriarch Naphtali was an abundant branch. Hence Moses says: “Naphtali is the fullness of those who receive; he will be filled with blessing from the Lord; he will possess the sea and the south-west.” In this he explains what Jacob had said, that he is a vine let loose, that is, freed from the chains of death through the grace of faith. In him is signified the people of God, called to the freedom of faith and the abundance of grace and spread throughout the whole world, a people which clothes the yoke of Christ with good fruit and twines about the wood of that true vine, that is, the mysteries of the Lord’s cross. It does not fear the danger of confessing him, but rather, even when set in the midst of persecutions, glories in the name of Christ.

He is truly let loose from chains who is bound by no tie of fear. Hence the prophet too says: “They will go out and leap like calves loosed from their bonds.” And so he puts forth beauty in his offspring, because, set down in a place of pasture and reared beside the water of refreshment, he brings forth through the sacraments of his regeneration the goodly beauty of the Word and is taken up into that most beautiful grace of Christ, who is able to increase the loveliness of your beauty.

Indeed, he who is beautiful above all gives what he has, for no one can give what he does not have. That is why it was said: “The Lord reigns, he has put on beauty.” For he put on beauty through the grace of the Church, which laid aside the foulness of all her sins in that washing and shone with the splendor of heavenly grace. And so the Bridegroom says of her: “Who is this who looks forth like the dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, a marvel like an adorned array?”

Now, to conclude our account with a kind of epilogue, just as divine Scripture itself concludes, let us set out the prophecy of holy Jacob concerning holy Joseph: “Joseph is my son, to be increased; my son, to be increased, envied; my younger son, return to me. Taking counsel against him, they reviled him, and the archers of the Lord aimed at him. But they were crushed together with the power of their bow, and the sinews of their arms and hands were loosed by the hand of the mighty one of Jacob; from there Israel prevailed, from the God of your father. And my God has helped you and blessed you with the blessing of heaven from above and with the blessing of the earth that holds all things, because of the blessing of the breasts and of the womb, the blessings of your father and your mother. He has prevailed over the blessings of the abiding mountains and over the desires of the everlasting hills: they will be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the brothers over whom he ruled.”

Why did the father honor his son Joseph more richly than all his other sons, if not because he saw prefigured in him the mysteries of Christ? So, blessing the one who was awaited rather than the one who was seen, he said: “Joseph is my son, to be increased.” Who is to be increased but Christ, whose grace always grows and whose glory has no end to its advance? Of him John also says: “He must increase, but I must decrease,” because through that saving and perfect name of his, grace has been heaped up and has abounded in this world. “My son, to be increased”: and because his brothers saw him grow, they began to envy him. And the Joseph who is understood spiritually also [?] incurred jealousy from those he cherished most. Indeed he said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” And they said: “We do not know where he is from.” He healed them, and they denied him.

“My younger son,” he says. Truly younger, since he was almost the last-born. Indeed Scripture also says: “Jacob loved him, because he was the son of his old age.” This too refers to Christ. For as the world was growing old and already sinking toward its setting, the Son of God dawned upon it and came late, through the childbearing of the virgin Mary. As a son of old age, in accordance with the mystery, he took up a body, he who was always with the Father before the ages. Hence [?] says

the Father to him: “Return to me,” calling him back from earth to heaven, the one he had sent for our salvation. And so, by raising up his only-begotten Son, he made void the counsel of those who reviled him (hence Isaiah too says: “Vain is the counsel of your spirit”), and he undid all the insults they aimed at him like arrows shot from a bow. He crushed the power of those who trusted in their own strength and not in God. “From there,” he says, “Israel prevailed, from the God of your father. And my God has helped you.” Who is it that strengthened Israel and helped the Son, if not God the Father alone, who said: “Jacob my servant, I will uphold him; Israel my chosen, my soul will receive him”?

“And he blessed him with the blessing of heaven from above and with the blessing of the earth that holds all things.” For he subjected all things to him, heavenly things as the blessing of heaven and earthly things as the blessing of the earth, so that he might rule over both men and angels.

And so, he says, in that seemingly contemptible body you prevailed, “because of the blessing of the breasts and of the womb, the blessings of your father and your mother.” By “breasts” he meant either the two Testaments, in one of which he was announced and in the other shown forth (and “breasts” is well said, since the Son reared us, nourished as it were on a spiritual milk, and offered us to God); or he means the breasts of Mary, which were truly blessed, with which the holy Virgin poured out a drink of milk for the people of the Lord. Hence that woman in the Gospel also says: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked!” As for his saying “the blessing of the womb, of your father and your mother,” if we wish to understand the womb of Mary alone, the reason why he joined the two blessings together will remain hidden, for he could have spoken of the mother’s womb alone. But I think it finer to understand, according to the spiritual mystery, both generations of the Lord Jesus, according to his divinity and according to his flesh, since he was begotten of the Father before the ages. Hence the Father also says: “My heart has poured forth a good word,” because he proceeded from that innermost and incomprehensible substance of the Father and is always in him. Hence the evangelist also says: “No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known.” Just as the bosom of the Father is understood spiritually as a kind of inner secret of the Father’s love and nature, in which the Son always is, so too the womb of the Father is the spiritual womb of his inner mystery, from which the Son proceeded as from a womb that gives birth. Indeed, we read variously now of the Father’s womb, now of his heart, from which he poured forth the Word, now of his mouth, from which righteousness proceeded and from which wisdom came forth, as Wisdom herself says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High.” So, since no single thing is fixed upon and all of them express one thing, it signifies the spiritual mystery of the Father’s begetting rather than some bodily member. But just as we understand that generation from the Father, so too, for the completion of the faith, let us understand the generation from Mary when the mother’s womb is blessed, that is, the virginal womb of Mary, which brought forth for us the Lord Jesus. Of it the Father says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and before you came forth from your mother’s womb, I sanctified you.” So the prophet declared a twofold substance in Christ, of divinity and of flesh, the one from the Father, the other from the Virgin, yet in such a way that he was not deprived of his divinity when he was born of the Virgin and was in the body.

Hence he also grew strong “over all the mountains and the desires of the everlasting hills.” For he shone forth above all those men of lofty merit, the patriarchs, prophets and apostles, and even beyond the sun, the moon and the archangels, like the light of heaven, as he himself says: “The disciple is not above his teacher, nor the servant above his master.” For which of those to whom he himself gave what they were had all things subjected to him? In him all his saints are blessed, because he is above the heads of all, the head of all (“for the head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ”), and above the crowns of all, because he is the crown that towers over all things. But he is the highest crown of the righteous, whom he calls brothers, won through grace and through a kind of fellowship of regeneration. Hence by Joseph’s “brothers” we understand rather those of whom he says in the psalm: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will sing to you.”

Moses too, when he was about to complete the course of this life and was blessing the tribe of Joseph, was certainly not blessing that Joseph who was already dead, but Christ, as you have it written of Joseph: “His land is from the blessing of the Lord, from the bounds of heaven and from the dew and from the depths of the springs below, and from the course of the sun made according to its seasons, and from the meeting of the months, and from the top of the mountains from the beginning, and from the top of the everlasting hills, and in the season of the fullness of the earth; and may what comes from him who was seen in the bush come upon the head of Joseph and upon his crown. He is honored among his brothers. The firstborn of the bull is his beauty, the horns of the unicorn. With them he will toss the nations together, to the ends of the earth. These are the ten thousands of Ephraim and these the thousands of Manasseh.”

It is the same blessing, which holds the whole fullness of things heavenly and earthly and the special grace of Christ, who was seen in the bush and said to Moses himself: “Take off the sandals from your feet.” He is God over all, for he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he himself might hold the first place, because in him it pleased all fullness to dwell. And therefore the privilege of this blessing, from the height of heaven to the ends of the earth, is granted to him alone. For he is before all, and in him all things hold together; through the blood of his cross he also made peace for all things, whether on earth or in heaven. Holy Joseph, bearing his type, is fittingly blessed, so that he is honored among his brothers.

“The firstborn of the bull is his beauty, having the horns of the unicorn, with which he will toss the nations.” He is indeed a good bull, an offering for sins and a victim for the whole world, that he might make peace for all things. His beauty is holy, for every firstborn is holy, as we have shown elsewhere; that is why Levi deserved to be called firstborn, not by order of age but by the privilege of sacred succession. And truly his beauty is holy, of whom it is written at his rising: “Fair in form beyond the sons of men,” because he is the firstborn from the dead, “having the horns of the unicorn.” But since he said “horns,” we must ask why he wrote “of the unicorn,” especially since, as experts say, the unicorn itself is not found among the kinds of wild beasts. And so we ought rather to take it as the one Word, because the substantial Word of God is one, not many words. Hence Hannah also says: “The Lord judges the ends of the earth; he will give strength to the king and exalt the horn of his anointed.” And Isaiah says: “My beloved had a vineyard on a horn in a fertile place,” because the Church flourishes in the only-begotten Son of God, holding the one Word of God, in whom is the fullness of power and wisdom, and by whose richness the crop of faith has sprung up. This Word the saints follow.

“The ten thousands,” he says, “of Ephraim and the thousands of Manasseh,” that is, that he should rule over both Jews and Gentiles and gain for himself the fullness of the Church from both peoples. That is why holy Jacob placed his right hand on Ephraim, because you read her saying in the Song of Songs: “My kinsman is white and ruddy, chosen out of ten thousand.” Indeed, the young women too extolled David, the ancestor of Mary, from whose line Christ was born through the Virgin’s childbearing, with ten thousands, but Saul with thousands, although out of reverence for the king they ought rather to have given him the greater weight. So whoever exalts the horn of Christ by confessing his glory himself also receives horns. Hence the saints too are called unicorns in a verse of the psalm: “And the beloved like a son of unicorns.” For just as in an animal of this kind the growth of horns signifies the advance to fuller age, so when horns begin to sprout from what we might call the head of our soul, they seem to signify an advance to more perfect virtue, and they keep growing until they are complete. With this horn the Lord Jesus crushed the nations, to stamp out superstition and restore salvation, as he himself says: “I will strike, and I will heal.” And so the prophet, as an imitator of this bull, says: “In you we will toss our enemies,” that is, by destroying every height that raises itself against the knowledge of God. That is also why, according to the Law, clean animals have horns, for the Law is spiritual. Those who can drive off the allurements of this world by the word of God and the practice of virtue seem to be armed with horns, as with the weapons of their head. And rightly the wonderful power of preaching is called a trumpet of horn, which rouses the good soldiers of Christ to battle, so that we may carry off spoils from our enemy, the devil. We are therefore in the battle line, and we see very many of our own held captive in the enemy camp. These we must free from the most grievous yoke of slavery.

The devil has a great many wolves, which he sends against the sheep of Christ. And so the spiritual Joseph, to protect his sheep, seized the very enemy who was coming to tear the sheep, the wolf, making Paul a teacher out of a persecutor. Of him Jacob speaks, as it is written: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he will still devour, and in the evening he will divide food to the princes.” He was a wolf when he scattered and devoured the sheep of the Church; but he who had come as a wolf became a shepherd. He was a wolf when he was Saul, when he entered houses and dragged men and women off to prison. He was a wolf when, breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, he asked the chief priests for letters so that he might fall upon the servants of Christ. Him, prowling like a wolf in the darkness of night, Jesus blinded with a flood of light. That is why Rachel, when she gave birth to Benjamin, called his name “son of my sorrow,” prophesying that Paul would come from that tribe, who would afflict the children of the Church in the time of his persecution and torment their mother with grievous pain. And yet, at a later time, the same man divided food to the princes, preaching the word of God to the Gentiles and calling very many to faith; through his preaching such men as [?] the proconsul Paulus and Publius, the chief man, received the grace of the Lord.

Moses too spoke beautifully when he blessed the tribe of Benjamin: “The beloved of the Lord will dwell in confidence, and God will overshadow him all his days, and the beloved of the Lord will rest between his shoulders.” He also became a chosen vessel, for he was converted in no other way than by the Lord’s mercy and love. Hence, attributing nothing to his own merit but giving all the credit to Christ, he himself says: “For I am the least of the apostles, unfit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not in want.” He dwelt in confidence in the house he had once laid waste; he dwelt in the tents of Christ, he who before had roamed the woods like a wolf. And God overshadowed him when Christ appeared to him. Though his eyes were open and he saw nothing, he nevertheless saw Christ. And rightly did he see him present, since he also heard him speaking. This overshadowing is not one of blindness, but of grace. Indeed, it is said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

“And he will rest between his shoulders,” that is, among good deeds and precious works. For you have it above too that Issachar put his shoulder to labor and became a farmer. Paul imitated him and set out the young plantings of faith, and so, like a good farmer, he said: “I planted, Apollos watered.”
